newsitem.title: USA: NC cities face power cost rise with deregulation.
newsitem.headline: NC cities face power cost rise with deregulation.

text.p: Deregulation of the electric utility industry could cause sharply higher rates for the 51 North Carolina municipal power systems which have borrowed to finance power plant construction in the state, according to Electricities of North Carolina Inc.

Electricities, the trade group representing North Carolina's 74 municipal power systems, said $6 billion in government debt is owed by the 51 systems which borrowed to help fund power plants being built by duke Energy Corp and Carolina Power & Light Co.

The group said its position is that deregulation is coming and the North Carolina Legislature should enact electric industry restructuring legislation that addresses deregulation on a statewide basis, the same basis on which it addressed the state's electric industry problems in 1975.
ElectriCities said restructuring legislation should provide for the recovery of 100 percent of stranded costs for all electric utilities, shared uniformly across all ratepayers in the state.
The group does not know how much of the $6 billion would be stranded costs with deregulation, spokeswoman Anna Turnage said. However, "a majority would probably be considered stranded," she added.

If the outstanding debt were assessed to only the ratepayers in the cities over a five-year period, the amount would broughly $0.10/kilowatt hour, which would more than double their existing rates, EletriCities said.
If the debt were uniformly assessed to all ratepayers in North Carolina over five years, the amount would be about $0.01/kilowatt hour, it added.

Explaining how this debt was incurred, the group cited the state legislature's 1975 determination it was desirable for the state, in order to ensure an adequate, reliable and economic supply of electric power, to authorize the municipalities in the state to jointly finance, develop, own and operate electric generation and transmisson facilities.

Following the action by the Legislature, the people of North Carolina, in 1977, approved an amendment to the North Carolina Constitution which authorized municipalities to jointly own and operate generation and transmission facilities with privately owned utilities.
